extracted.intended_audience: academics, scholars, and research administrators interested in grant peer review and disciplinary differences in evaluation (panel members, program officers, higher-education researchers).
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying how disciplinary epistemological cultures shape the criteria used to evaluate grant/fellowship proposals on multidisciplinary review panels, including dominant evaluative styles and specific quality dimensions valued by different fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive style (verstehen / contextual specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Values verstehen, attention to details, and contextual specificity in proposals (historically and culturally sensitive social science and humanistic research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobilized primarily by humanists, historians, and many social scientists; favors historically and culturally situated analyses rather than broad generalizations. Example: emphasis on careful mapping and attention to complexities of social experience. Antipattern: privileging abstract generalization at the expense of rich context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist style (reflexivity / giving voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizes proposals that 'give voice' to various groups and values reflexivity—consideration of the researcher's identity and commitments in shaping analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to anti-positivists and politically/socially engaged research; common among humanists and some historians. Guidance includes highlighting researcher positionality. Antipattern: presenting research as entirely neutral/objective without acknowledging standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivist style (generalizability / hypothesis testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favors generalizability and hypothesis testing, use of formal models and statistical frameworks to prove theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most used by social scientists (particularly political science, sociology, economics); values multiple cases and strong research design. Antipatterns: single-case storytelling without hypothesis testing or formal design is seen as weaker in these fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian style (instrumental knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Values only the production of instrumental / applied knowledge rather than theoretical or interpretative aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Least popular style; used by a minority of social scientists and some historians. Guidance: emphasize practical applications and policy relevance. Antipattern: privileging abstract interpretive insights with little practical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the proposed claims are valid—i.e., do methods and design support the inferences made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly named by panelists as a key standard; linked to parsimony and generalizability. Antipattern: drawing strong conclusions from weak or irrelevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for theories that are parsimonious—simple explanations that capture explanatory power without unnecessary complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as an important but secondary standard to validity in some social-science evaluations. Antipattern: overly baroque theoretical constructions that do not improve explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which findings/theory apply across different historical epochs or societies (not across extraordinarily different societies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued in positivist assessments; panels reward projects that can show broader applicability. Antipattern: claims of universal application drawn from a single narrowly contextualized case without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability / disconfirmability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability for results to be replicated or shown to be disprovable—'to have discomfirmable knowledge'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as crucial by some social-science panelists; links to systematic methods and clear empirical procedures. Antipattern: research presented as personal expressions with no possibility of independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on building systematic bodies of knowledge rather than isolated anecdotes or purely expressive work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued in fields that prize cumulative science; guidance includes methods and designs that produce comparable, organized results. Antipattern: idiosyncratic projects that do not contribute to cumulative understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to research design (multiple cases / strong design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for multiple-case studies and strong research design, especially in political science, sociology, and economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists from these fields are less comfortable with single-case or purely narrative projects; they expect explicit design choices that support causal inference. Antipattern: relying solely on storytelling without design that supports claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive / single-case comfort (storytelling / 'empirical dirty hands')
rubrics_metrics.description: Comfort with single-case, inductive approaches and 'empirical dirty hands'—deep immersion, narrative, and thick description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical of anthropology and history; values language proficiency, cultural knowledge, and time spent in the field. Antipattern: forcing statistical generalizability norms onto inductive, context-rich projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fieldwork competence (language, cultural knowledge, time in place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of language proficiency, knowledge of the culture, and significant time spent in the research location as markers of quality for ethnographic projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial for anthropological and certain historical research; panels expect demonstrated immersion. Antipattern: proposing fieldwork without demonstrated ability to access or understand the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor, analytic clarity, and argumentative precision (philosophy standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to make analytic distinctions, clarify positions in a novel way, rigorous working through implications, mastery of details, and a sense of larger-scale significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as philosophy's hallmark—'rigor' and 'ruthlessness' in argumentation. Antipattern: vague, unfocused, or unintelligible proposals that lack clear argumentative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal must explain why the work matters—its significance and contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists criticized some philosophy proposals for failing to explain significance; clarity about significance helps cross-disciplinary understanding. Antipattern: assuming significance is self-evident without articulating it to non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty of contribution; 'originality' is a central evaluative criterion but is manifested differently across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanists may value originality in approach or interpretive angle; panels often assess originality via study of new objects which can disadvantage philosophy where innovation often addresses traditional problems. Antipattern: equating originality only with new objects rather than novel conceptual moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocativeness / fascination over empirical truth (humanities preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanists may place originality and the potential to 'provoke really fascinating conversations' above empirical truth or provable claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanist reviewers may support projects that are compelling or thought-provoking even if they cannot be definitively proven. Antipattern: dismissing such projects for lack of empirical testability when their disciplinary value is interpretive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental / applied relevance (utilitarian criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Value placed on the production of applied, instrumental knowledge useful beyond academic theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When panels or reviewers favor utilitarian criteria, proposals should foreground practical outcomes and applications. Antipattern: emphasizing purely theoretical contributions when the panel expects applied impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive contextualization (evaluate by applicant's disciplinary norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice of evaluating a proposal using the criteria valued in the applicant's discipline rather than the reviewer's own disciplinary standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multidisciplinary panels often 'loosen' their own standards and give preference to applicant-discipline criteria to reach consensus; recommended to prevent unfair dismissal of discipline-specific work. Antipattern: imposing one's own field's standards on a proposal from another discipline without accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief about excellence (objective vs constructed / intersubjective consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers see 'excellence' as an objective property of a proposal or as constructed through panel interaction and intersubjective agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields influenced by post-structuralism (e.g., English) may view excellence as constructed and emphasize negotiated criteria; other fields see excellence as more objective. This stance affects willingness to defer or to seek consensus. Antipattern: assuming universal agreement on what constitutes excellence when disciplinary perspectives differ.
